Gloriously
glo'ri-us-ly
adv. (in a glorious manner; splendidly; with triumph)
From glorious, Latin gloriosus, from gloria, glory, renown, praise. The adverb appears three times in the Authorized Version, twice in the same song and once at the end of the world.

Biblical Definition

Gloriously is a word the Bible reserves for what God does, never for what man achieves. Its first two occurrences are the same line sung twice on the far shore of the Red Sea: “I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea” (Exo 15:1), and again from Miriam and the women with timbrels, “Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously” (Exo 15:21). Israel had not struck a blow. They had stood still and seen the salvation of the LORD, and the adverb belongs entirely to Him. The third occurrence closes the circle at the end of history: “Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously” (Isa 24:23). The sun itself is put out of countenance. Between the Red Sea and the reign in Zion the word does not wander into human hands once. That is the doctrine hidden in an adverb: glory is God's manner of acting, and the creature's only proper share in it is the singing. Moses asks the question the word answers: “Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?” (Exo 15:11).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines gloriously as in a glorious manner; splendidly; with great renown or dignity; illustriously.

expand to see more

GLO'RIOUSLY, adv. [from glorious.]

1. Splendidly; illustriously; with great renown or dignity.

He hath triumphed gloriously.

2. With great honor or magnificence.

The adverb in Scripture is used of the LORD's own acting and reigning, not of the creature's success.

Key Scripture

Exodus 15:1 — "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD, and spake, saying, I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea."

Exodus 15:21 — "And Miriam answered them, Sing ye to the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea."

Isaiah 24:23 — "Then the moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed, when the LORD of hosts shall reign in mount Zion, and in Jerusalem, and before his ancients gloriously."

Exodus 15:11 — "Who is like unto thee, O LORD, among the gods? who is like thee, glorious in holiness, fearful in praises, doing wonders?"

Modern Corruption

The adverb has been transferred from God's triumph to man's performance, which is the oldest theft in religion.

expand to see more

Every age wants the adverb for itself. The nation triumphs gloriously, the ministry grows gloriously, the believer overcomes gloriously. Exodus 15 will not lend the word. Israel's entire contribution at the sea was to be afraid and then to sing. When a church begins to describe its own works with the vocabulary Scripture reserves for God's acts, it has already started down the road to the joyous city of Isaiah 22 — loud, self-congratulating, and unaware of the measuring line.

Isaiah 24:23 supplies the other guard. The sun is ashamed. Whatever glory the creature has is borrowed light, and borrowed light is put out when the Lender appears. This is why the Reformed instinct ends every doctrine at soli Deo gloria: not as a pious signature at the bottom of the page, but as the only honest grammar. Man may sing gloriously of God. He may not triumph gloriously in himself.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ga'ah (H1342), to rise up, to be exalted, to triumph; Greek endoxos (G1741), glorious; Latin gloria, renown.

expand to see more

Hebrew ga'oh ga'ah (H1342) — literally rising He has risen, the doubled verb the Authorized Version renders triumphed gloriously; Exodus 15:1.

Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, substance; the noun standing behind the adverb's whole idea.

Greek endoxos (G1741) — held in honour, splendid; the Septuagint's word at Exodus 15:11.

Latin gloria — renown, praise; Webster's root, and the last word of the Reformed solas.

Hebrew neged zeqenaw kabod — before his ancients gloriously; Isaiah 24:23, glory shown to the elders of the redeemed.

Usage

"“He hath triumphed gloriously” — sung by Moses, then by Miriam; the sea did the arguing."

"“The moon shall be confounded, and the sun ashamed” — borrowed light goes out when the Lender reigns."

"“Glorious in holiness, fearful in praises” — the holiness is what makes the glory terrible."
